steps.body: Here's rounding's real job: **fast, good-enough answers**. When a story asks "about how many," round the players to friendly numbers FIRST, then do one easy computation. The answer wears its "about" badge proudly — you met this move guarding word problems in earlier courses.
Feel the size before touching any exact digits.

widget.prompt: One stadium section holds 289 fans, another holds 512. Slide to estimate the total fans.
widget.lowFeedback: Too few — the second section ALONE holds about 500. Slide up.
widget.highFeedback: That's the whole stadium! Three hundred plus five hundred lands under a thousand — come back down.
widget.successFeedback: About 800 — think 300 + 500. The exact answer (801) was hiding one step away the whole time.

predict.prompt: 289 + 512, rounded to friendly hundreds, is about…
predict.reveal: 289 leans up to 300 and 512 leans down to 500: about 800. Rounding both DOWN to 200 + 500 ignores that 289 is a whisker from 300 — estimates round each number to its nearest friend.

cml.actionGoal: Manipulate the model and track how it represents estimation.
invariants: The manipulated model and the mathematical relationship for estimation must stay consistent.
misconceptions: Changing a visible feature without preserving the relationship that defines estimation.
cml.counterfactualPrompt: What change would make the model stop representing the same mathematical relationship?

steps.body: Estimation is a tool — know when to reach for it.
explanationVariants: Round when 'about' answers the real question — enough money? enough chairs? — and exactness would just cost time.
Estimates trade a little precision for a lot of speed; that trade is only smart when precision isn't the point.

widget.prompt: When is rounding-to-estimate the RIGHT move?

options.label: When 'about' is good enough — like checking money
options.feedback: Estimates shine when the question is really a yes/no or a rough size — speed matters, exactness doesn't.

options.label: Always — exact answers are old-fashioned now
options.feedback: Try paying a bill with an estimate! When the question needs the true number, exact work is the only honest answer.

options.label: Never — rounding is basically just lying
options.feedback: An estimate labeled 'about' tells the truth — it promises a size, not a digit-perfect count. Lying would be calling it exact.

options.label: Only when the numbers happen to end in 5
options.feedback: Any number rounds — 287, 412, whatever the story brings. The 5s only matter for tie-breaking, not for whether to estimate.

steps.body: Estimates also work as **guards** — the same trick from the word-problem workshop. For 512 − 289, think 500 − 300 = 200. Now any "exact" answer far from 200 is busted on sight: 723 fails instantly (it's bigger than what you started with!).
Build the guard for a subtraction.
explanationVariants: 512 → 500 (tens digit 1) and 289 → 300 (tens digit 8); the friendly version is 500 − 300 = 200.
The exact answer, 223, sits comfortably near the 200 guard — that's the guard confirming it.

widget.prompt: Estimate 512 − 289 by rounding each number to the nearest hundred first.

commonErrors.feedback: 223 is the EXACT difference — nice arithmetic, but the estimate wants the rounded players: 500 − 300.
300 rounded 289 DOWN to 200 — but its tens digit is 8, well past the middle. 289 climbs to 300, making 500 − 300.
800 ADDED the rounded numbers. The story subtracts — the estimate must run the same operation as the exact work.

widget.fallbackFeedback: Round both first (512 → ?, 289 → ?), then subtract the friendly versions.

steps.body: The guard on duty: 313 + 296, estimate ≈ 600. Which offered answers survive it?

widget.prompt: Sort each offered answer: does it pass the ≈600 size check, or does the estimate bust it?

items.feedback: 609 sits right beside 600 — the guard waves it through. (It's also the exact answer.)
509 is a whole hundred below the guard's 600 — somewhere a hundred went missing. Busted.
899 overshoots the guard by almost 300 — no small slip makes that. Busted on sight.
613 passes the SIZE check even though it isn't the exact answer (609 is). Guards catch big blunders, not small slips — that's their honest limit.

widget.missFeedback: Compare each to 600: within a few dozen steps passes; a hundred or more off is busted.
widget.successFeedback: The guard cleared 609 and 613, busted 509 and 899 — estimates catch the big mistakes and admit they can't see the small ones.

steps.body: The strongest estimate: round in the SAFE direction.
explanationVariants: Round her money DOWN (412 → 400) and the price UP (289 → 300): if the shrunken money still beats the inflated price, the real answer must too.
400 > 300 with the odds stacked AGAINST her — so the true 412 vs 289 is a certain yes, no exact subtraction needed.

widget.prompt: Maya has $412; a bike costs $289. Using rounding, can she afford it — for CERTAIN?

options.label: Yes — her money DOWN (400) beats price UP (300)
options.feedback: Safe-direction rounding: shrink what you have, inflate what it must beat. If it still wins, the real answer is guaranteed.

options.label: No — 289 rounds to 300, and that's a lot
options.feedback: Compare it to her side: even shortchanged to 400, Maya clears 300 with a hundred to spare.

options.label: Can't be certain without exact subtraction
options.feedback: Usually true — but rounding AGAINST yourself creates certainty: if the unfair version passes, the fair one must.

options.label: Yes, because bikes are usually pretty cheap
options.feedback: Bike trivia isn't math! The certainty comes from the numbers: down-rounded 400 beats up-rounded 300.

steps.body: One more round-and-add warm-up, ADDING this time, before the two shelf walls.
explanationVariants: 340 rounds down to 300 (tens digit 4); 270 rounds up to 300 (tens digit 7). Add the rounded pair: 300 + 300 = 600.
Two separate rounds first — both land on 300 — then one easy addition: 600.

widget.prompt: Round 340 to its nearest hundred, round 270 to its nearest hundred, then add the two rounded numbers. What do you get?

commonErrors.feedback: 610 is the EXACT sum — round each first: 340→300, 270→300, then add: 300+300=600.
340's tens digit is 4, in the round-DOWN club — it stays at 300, not up to 400. 300+300=600.
270's tens digit is 7, in the round-UP club — it climbs to 300, not down to 200. 300+300=600.

widget.fallbackFeedback: Round each number to its nearest hundred first (340→?, 270→?), then add the two rounded hundreds.

steps.body: A library wall, estimated end to end.
hints: Round each shelf wall to its nearest hundred — tens digits decide.
explanationVariants: Both walls round to the same friendly 400 — one from below, one from above — and the estimate becomes a doubling.

widget.prompt: A library has 385 books on one shelf wall and 428 on another. Round each to the nearest hundred, then add, to estimate the total.

commonErrors.feedback: 813 is the EXACT total — the estimate wants the rounded walls: 400 + 400.
700 rounded 385 DOWN to 300 — but its tens digit is 8. 385 climbs to 400.
900 rounded 428 UP to 500 — but its tens digit is just 2. 428 stays down at 400.

widget.fallbackFeedback: Two rounds (385 → ?, 428 → ?), then one addition of hundreds.

steps.body: Rounding earns its keep in the real world now.
takeaways: For 'about' questions: round the players first, then compute once.
Estimates guard exact work — they catch big blunders and honestly miss small slips.
Safe-direction rounding (against yourself) can settle yes/no questions with certainty.
steps.teaser: next chapter: adding and subtracting to 1,000 — with friendly-number jumps that make it feel easy.

concept.body: Quick rewind. An "about how many" question invites the friendly version: **round each player, then do ONE easy step**. 198 + 304? Think 200 + 300 = 500. The exact answer lives close to the estimate — that's the whole point.

explanationVariants: Both numbers sit a step or two from friendly hundreds — the estimate almost computes itself.

options.label: About 500 — think 200 + 300
options.feedback: Friendly players, one easy add. (The exact 502 is two steps away.)

options.label: Exactly 502 — 'about' still demands exact work
options.feedback: 502 is right — but 'about' INVITES the friendly version. Estimation's job is speed: 200 + 300 in one glance.

options.label: About 600
options.feedback: 600 rounds 304 up to 400 — but 304 sits just past 300. Both players round to the near hundreds: 200 and 300.
